title: Architectural design and the brain: Effects of ceiling height and perceived enclosure on beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions

findings.antecedent: rooms with high ceilings (compared to low ceilings)
findings.consequent: beauty judgments (likelihood to be judged as beautiful)
findings.mechanism: rooms with higher ceilings might be preferred because they facilitate greater levels of visuospatial exploration and attention
findings.quote: participants were more likely to judge spaces as beautiful if they had high than low ceilings

findings.antecedent: rooms with high ceilings (compared to low ceilings)
findings.mechanism: neural dissociation between liking and wanting (Berridge, 1995) might lead to a differentiation of how ceiling height...affect beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions
findings.quote: rooms with higher ceilings were no more likely to be entered than rooms with lower ceilings

findings.antecedent: open rooms (low perceived enclosure, compared to enclosed rooms)
findings.consequent: beauty judgments (likelihood to be judged as beautiful)
findings.mechanism: open rooms afford a greater degree of perceived visual and locomotive permeability
findings.quote: participants were more likely to judge spaces as beautiful if they were open than enclosed

findings.antecedent: enclosed rooms (high perceived enclosure, compared to open rooms)
findings.mechanism: a reduction in perceived visual and locomotive permeability characteristic of enclosed spaces might elicit an emotional reaction that accompanies exit decisions.
findings.quote: more likely to opt to exit them if they were enclosed than open.

findings.antecedent: rooms with high ceilings (compared to low ceilings)
findings.consequent: left precuneus (BA 19) activation during beauty judgment
findings.mechanism: rooms with higher ceilings might be preferred because they facilitate greater levels of visuospatial exploration and attention
findings.quote: significant activation in left precuneus (BA 19) (T = 4.08, d(T/√N) = .96)

findings.antecedent: rooms with high ceilings (compared to low ceilings)
findings.consequent: left middle frontal gyrus (BA 6) activation during beauty judgment
findings.mechanism: rooms with higher ceilings might be preferred because they facilitate greater levels of visuospatial exploration and attention

findings.consequent: left middle temporal gyrus (BA 21) activation during beauty judgment
findings.mechanism: involvement of left middle temporal gyrus (BA 21) might be related to a greater representation of perceived visual motion in open rooms.
findings.quote: significant activation in left middle temporal gyrus (BA 21) (T = 4.17, d = .98)

findings.consequent: right superior temporal gyrus (BA 22) activation during beauty judgment
findings.mechanism: temporal dynamics of visual processing might be influenced differently by open vs. enclosed spaces

findings.antecedent: rooms with high ceilings (compared to low ceilings)
findings.mechanism: neural dissociation between liking and wanting (Berridge, 1995) might lead to a differentiation of how ceiling height...affect beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions
findings.quote: the contrast of high ceilings-low ceilings did not reveal any significant activation

findings.consequent: anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC, BA 24) activation during approach-avoidance decisions
findings.mechanism: part of the reason for opting to exit enclosed spaces might be related to the experience of fear
findings.quote: enclosed-open contrast revealed significantly greater activation in...anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) region... (T = 6.63, d = 1.56)

stimuli.description: 200 photographs of interior architectural spaces, balanced for ceiling height (high/low), perceived enclosure (open/enclosed), and contour (curvilinear/rectilinear).

limitations: Familiarity with standard ceiling heights might have influenced beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions.
Stimuli were not controlled for other variables such as light and color, potentially introducing confounds.
The study did not distinguish between visual and locomotive permeability in stimuli, which might have different impacts on beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions.
